assumptions: The initial beachhead is small commercial-building and multi-unit retrofit finance, not the already mature household OZE-credit channel.
The company remains asset-light, does not hold credit risk, and launches covered activity only after obtaining the required legal structure, registrations, disclosures, and lender approvals.
Access to the founder's family renewable-energy company enables a bounded pilot but does not itself prove installer exclusivity, repeatable external distribution, or scalable quote volume.
The proposed 1%-3% lender-paid fee, 300-900 PLN monthly installer fee, 65%-85% gross margin, and 9-18 month payback are hypotheses rather than established economics.
Neutral multi-lender participation, consented outcome-data rights, funded conversion, and commercial retrofit deal frequency remain unknown until directly tested.
The founder keeps the corporate role during validation, contributes no more than five hours per day, and delegates specialist legal and compliance work within the stated initial-capital envelope.

factors.name: Core insight
factors.rationale: Embedding finance at the point where an acceptable retrofit quote stalls is coherent, and the bank and installer evidence confirms that this behavior already exists at scale. The differentiated insight is narrower—neutral multi-lender routing and document orchestration for smaller commercial projects—but research establishes that only as a plausible gap, not a demonstrated market misunderstanding.

factors.name: Customer pain and willingness to pay
factors.rationale: Upfront cost is a credible purchase blocker, while existing installer-assisted credit and Inbank's reported loan volume show real borrower use of retrofit finance. That supports underlying pain and willingness to finance, but it does not establish the abandonment rate, commercial-building demand, lender willingness to pay this intermediary, or installer willingness to pay a software fee.

factors.name: Business model and economics
factors.rationale: An asset-light funded-deal fee plus optional workflow subscription could provide good cash conversion and operating leverage without balance-sheet risk. However, commission schedules, funded conversion, CAC, integration expense, adverse-decision support, retention, gross margin, and owner earnings are all unresolved; scaled incumbents may also compress fees and raise channel-acquisition costs. The proposed founder-net-worth path is therefore possible in form but unsupported by the available economics.

factors.name: Market and beachhead
factors.rationale: SME installers serving smaller commercial and multi-unit retrofits are a reasonably specific starting segment, and policy direction supports continued renovation activity. Yet the evidence neither sizes this segment nor establishes project frequency, ticket size, finance abandonment, or underserved volume; the better-evidenced household segment is already mature and crowded.

factors.name: Competitive position and domination potential
factors.rationale: A neutral router could aggregate fragmented installers and offer choice across lenders, but no lender neutrality, exclusive placement, or superior conversion has been secured. Credit Agricole and BNP already embed credit in merchant flows, Inbank reports a network exceeding 200 partners, and Energa with SGB can bundle advice, finance, and delivery, leaving the candidate without an evidenced route to a dominant beachhead.

factors.name: Expansion potential
factors.rationale: If the commercial wedge works, the workflow could extend across more installers, lenders, retrofit categories, quoting platforms, multi-unit buildings, and nearby EU markets. Those adjacencies are logically available, but each adds lender, regulatory, integration, and local-distribution work, and expansion is contingent on proving the first segment rather than being unlocked today.

factors.name: Defensibility and durability
factors.rationale: Exclusive quote placement and consented quote-to-funding outcomes could create switching costs and a matching-data loop. Both control points are currently assumptions, while lenders and large energy providers already own relevant relationships and data, can copy workflow features, and can terminate or bypass an intermediary; policy-linked workflows can also change.

factors.name: Strength of advantage
factors.rationale: Multi-lender matching and unified documentation may improve approval probability or convenience versus a tied lender. The research provides no measured conversion, speed, price, or workflow advantage, while an incumbent already advertises electronic agreements and decisions as fast as 15 minutes, so there is not yet a demonstrated behavior-changing improvement.

factors.name: Timing and momentum
factors.rationale: EU renovation policy, explicit support for one-stop assistance, and substantial incumbent green-loan activity create favorable category momentum. Timing is moderated by the maturity of existing embedded channels and by changing programme details, illustrated by the expiration of the enhanced BGK grant application window.

factors.name: Distribution
factors.rationale: The family installation company is a concrete, low-cost pilot route at the purchase moment and is unusually well matched to the founder. Beyond that test bed, there is no evidence that installers will grant exclusivity, adopt a neutral router, or pay monthly, and incumbent lenders, utilities, and their established partner networks already occupy the same distribution surface.

factors.name: Execution and risks
factors.rationale: The founder has relevant data, automation, finance, and installer access, and an asset-light pilot can fit the stated capital and part-time constraints if specialist work is delegated. Execution still requires regulated-process design, lender contracting, integrations, consent and data governance, exception support, and partner sales; legal perimeter and a sustainable two-to-three-hour daily operating load remain unverified rather than impossible.

main_structural_strength: The business can test a high-value finance intervention exactly at the quote decision point through a founder-accessible installer, while regulated lenders retain underwriting and credit risk; if repeated beyond the pilot, the workflow could generate valuable quote-to-funding outcome data.
primary_score_limiter: There is no evidenced economic or distribution wedge against scaled embedded-finance incumbents: neutral lender participation, commissions, commercial-project volume, installer adoption, conversion lift, support cost, exclusivity, and reusable outcome-data rights are all unresolved.
strongest_disconfirming_evidence: Inbank reports more than 200 Polish OZE partners and more than 80,000 prior green-installation loans, while Credit Agricole and BNP already embed fast credit in installer or merchant flows and Energa with SGB bundle technical delivery and financing; together this directly contradicts an open-channel or weak-incumbent thesis.
evidence_needed_for_higher_score: Obtain a legal-perimeter memo and then a live commercial-building pilot with at least two lenders on written, preferably non-exclusive terms disclosing commissions and data rights; measure eligible quote volume, abandonment, approval and funding conversion by lender, time-to-fund, installer activation and retention, CAC, integration and exception-support cost, gross margin, and whether multi-lender routing materially outperforms a tied-lender baseline.
highest_value_structural_change: Replace dependence on exclusive lender-paid placement with an installer-paid system of record for commercial and multi-unit retrofit eligibility, documentation, subsidy coordination, and lender-ready export; treat lender referral revenue as incremental. This would move the control point into a recurring workflow the company can own even when a lender changes, while still preserving multi-lender upside if validation supports it.
